newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Wives play minor roles in British election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Wives play minor roles in British election.

text.p: Cherie Blair is the sphinx of husband Tony's election campaign.
Everyone recognises the smiling wife of Britain's opposition leader but few voters know much about her.

Britain has been quick to adopt the tactics of U.S.-style politics with their spin doctors and daily press briefings, but the main political parties have stopped short of giving the candidate's wives major roles in the campaign.
Cherie and Prime Minister John Major's wife, Norma, are carrying out non-speaking, strictly supporting roles.
Elizabeth Dole routinely stepped in for husband Bob in his failed bid for the top U.S. job -- some say she overshadowed him -- and Hillary Clinton garnered her fair share of headlines.

But Cherie, a top notch lawyer whose salary dwarfs that of her husband, and Norma, an accomplished author and veteran political wife, have barely uttered a word during the campaign for the May 1 election.

Both women have dutifully accompanied their men on the campaign trail, smiling through factory tours and shaking hands with supporters, but neither has ventured out on her own or commented on the major issues.
"Tony Blair is standing in the election, not his wife," said a Labour Party spokesman when questioned about Cherie's place.
According to campaign officials Cherie's back seat role is of her own choosing.
"It's a matter of what she wants to do," said her political adviser Fiona Millar, who also happens to be the partner of Tony Blair's press spokesman Alistair Campbell.
There is little doubt the strong emotions inspired by Glenys Kinnock, the outspoken wife of Blair's predecessor as Labour leader, Neil Kinnock, underpins Cherie's safety-first approach.
KEEPING HER OWN COUNSEL
Cherie, a mother of three, uses her maiden name in her professional capacity and is tipped as a future high court judge. But she has put her work on hold until after the election.
Considered one of the country's top legal minds, she was a radical in her young days. If she has strong opinions on taxes, Europe and sleaze, she is keeping them to herself.
"Cherie is a very private person, that's what it boils down to," said Millar.
Her only public comments were at a recent awards dinner when she was voted Legal Personality of the Year by a British professional magazine.

"I'm not so immodest to think that my recent high profile is totally unconnected with one Mr Tony Blair or even the events going to happen on the first of May," she said in her acceptance speech. "I only hope he does as well in his ballot as I did in mine."
Asked if her success could be a disadvantage to her husband, she replied: "I don't know about that."

Norma Major, a decade older than 42-year-old Cherie, has made no secret of her distaste for the political life, preferring to remain in her rural home while her husband attends to state affairs at 10 Downing Street.
She has admitted she would not have changed the past five years which took her to many far off places and gave her the opportunity to meet some extraordinary people.
But no one is quite sure how Cherie feels about the public life that will be thrust upon her if Labour, as expected, wins the election. Nor are they likely to.
"She doesn't give interviews. She doesn't feel comfortable talking about herself," explained Millar, dismissing suggestions that Labour has not been using Cherie to their best advantage.
"It's a very important time for both of them and I think they want to be together," she added.

Journalists who have accompanied the Blairs on the campaign trail say Cherie is popular with the crowds but is not a natural campaigner. She tries hard to do well and to give the impression that she is enjoying herself. The press respectS her wishes to maintain a low profile and never question her directly.
"It's difficult to get an impression of her because she is there as a prop," said one seasoned political reporter.
Apart from Glenys Kinnock, no other British wife in recent memory has played a dominant role in a British election.
Cherie, and certainly Norma, are unlikely to change that.
